name: Oliver Chen
chief_complaint: Ear pain and fever for 2 days - child pulling at right ear and crying
opening_statement: (Parent speaking) Oliver has been crying and pulling at his right ear for the past 2 days. He's had a fever and isn't sleeping well. He had a cold last week that seemed to be getting better, but then this ear pain started.
emotional_baseline: Child: distressed, irritable, crying. Parent: concerned but cooperative

socrates.site: Right ear (child pulling at right ear)
socrates.onset: 2 days ago, following upper respiratory tract infection 1 week ago
socrates.character: Continuous pain, child crying and irritable
socrates.associated: Fever, irritability, reduced feeding, tugging at ear
socrates.timing: Constant, worse at night (lying down increases middle ear pressure)

rag_citation.source: eTG Pediatrics 6.4.1: Acute Otitis Media - Clinical Features
rag_citation.quote: Acute otitis media presents with ear pain (otalgia), fever, and irritability in children - often follows viral URTI
Fever in AOM indicates middle ear inflammation - typically resolves within 24-48h of appropriate treatment
Young children with AOM may not verbalize ear pain - present with irritability, sleep disturbance, and ear tugging
Reduced feeding in AOM results from pain with swallowing (eustachian tube pressure changes)

past_medical_history: Up-to-date with immunizations (including pneumococcal vaccine PCV13)
medications: Paracetamol 15mg/kg PRN for fever/pain (parent giving 240mg q6h - appropriate dose for 16kg child)
family_history: No significant family history. Older sibling (age 5) healthy.

social_history.living_situation: Lives with both parents and older sibling, attends daycare 3 days/week
social_history.development: Meeting developmental milestones appropriately for age
social_history.daycare: Yes - 3 days per week (increased URTI exposure)

vitals.general_appearance: Irritable, crying when ears examined, consolable

ent_examination.right_ear: Tympanic membrane BULGING and ERYTHEMATOUS (red), loss of normal landmarks (light reflex absent), REDUCED MOBILITY on pneumatic otoscopy - DIAGNOSTIC OF ACUTE OTITIS MEDIA
ent_examination.left_ear: Tympanic membrane normal appearance, mobile, light reflex present
ent_examination.nose: Clear nasal discharge (resolving URTI), no purulent discharge
ent_examination.throat: Mild pharyngeal erythema (viral URTI), tonsils not enlarged, no exudate

examination_findings.general: Alert, interactive when not examining ears, no signs of severe illness
examination_findings.cardiovascular: Normal heart sounds, no murmurs, capillary refill <2 seconds, well perfused
examination_findings.respiratory: Clear breath sounds bilaterally, no wheeze/creps, no respiratory distress
examination_findings.neurological: Alert, age-appropriate behavior, no meningism (neck supple, no photophobia), fontanelle closed (normal for age 3)

investigations.clinical_diagnosis: Acute otitis media is a CLINICAL diagnosis - no investigations required in uncomplicated cases
investigations.tympanometry: Not routinely performed in acute setting (used for chronic OME - otitis media with effusion)
investigations.fbc: NOT indicated in uncomplicated AOM (no benefit for management decision)
investigations.blood_culture: NOT indicated (unless septic, toxic appearance, or immunocompromised)

expected_management: DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA (ALL 3 REQUIRED FOR AOM DIAGNOSIS):
2. Middle ear effusion (bulging TM, reduced mobility) ✓
- Ibuprofen 10mg/kg q6-8h (max 40mg/kg/day) - can add if paracetamol insufficient
- Age <2 years with bilateral AOM ✗ (unilateral only)
- Strategy: Analgesia + review in 24-48h, prescribe antibiotics if no improvement
- First-line: Amoxicillin 50mg/kg/day divided TDS × 5 days (e.g., 250mg TDS for 16kg child)
- If penicillin allergy: Cefaclor 20mg/kg/day divided TDS × 5 days
- Duration: 5 days (vs 10 days previously - shorter course equally effective with less resistance)
- AOM often viral or self-limiting (60-80% resolve without antibiotics)
- Return if fever persists >48h, worsening symptoms, or systemically unwell
- Delayed prescription strategy: give script but advise to fill only if no improvement in 48h
9. Red flags for parents - return immediately if:
- Facial weakness (facial nerve palsy - rare complication)
10. Review in 24-48 hours (phone or in-person) - assess clinical response
11. If symptoms persist >48h despite antibiotics: consider treatment failure (change to amoxicillin-clavulanate)
12. Hearing check in 3 months if recurrent AOM or persistent OME (rule out conductive hearing loss)
13. Pneumococcal vaccination up-to-date ✓ (reduces AOM incidence by 6-7%)
14. Influenza vaccination (annual) - reduces viral URTI → secondary AOM
15. Minimize daycare if recurrent AOM (though not always practical)
17. Grommets (tympanostomy tubes) - only if recurrent AOM (≥3 episodes in 6 months or ≥4 in 12 months) or persistent OME with hearing loss

critical_errors.error: Prescribed antibiotics immediately in well child >2 years with unilateral AOM (watch-and-wait appropriate)
critical_errors.explanation: Over-prescribing antibiotics contributes to antimicrobial resistance - watch-and-wait safe in well children >2y with unilateral AOM

critical_errors.error: Failed to provide adequate analgesia (pain relief is PRIORITY treatment in AOM)
critical_errors.explanation: Analgesia more important than antibiotics for symptom relief - inadequate pain control causes unnecessary suffering

critical_errors.error: Prescribed amoxicillin-clavulanate as first-line (instead of amoxicillin alone)
critical_errors.explanation: Amoxicillin-clavulanate has more side effects (diarrhea) without superior efficacy in uncomplicated AOM - reserve for treatment failure
5-day course equally effective as 10-day in children >2 years - shorter course improves compliance, reduces side effects

critical_errors.error: Missed mastoiditis (swelling behind ear, displaced pinna) - requires urgent IV antibiotics and imaging
critical_errors.explanation: Mastoiditis is life-threatening AOM complication requiring hospitalization - delays increase risk of intracranial spread

critical_errors.error: Failed to check immunization status (pneumococcal vaccine reduces AOM risk)
critical_errors.explanation: Opportunistic check of immunization status - catch-up vaccinations reduce future AOM risk

fracp_reviews.clinical_accuracy: Excellent - realistic AOM presentation in preschool child with watch-and-wait appropriateness clearly outlined
fracp_reviews.difficulty_appropriate: Yes - Easy difficulty appropriate (common GP presentation, straightforward diagnosis/management)
fracp_reviews.rag_citations_correct: Yes - eTG 6.4 citations verified and accurate
fracp_reviews.feedback: Excellent pediatrics persona. Good emphasis on analgesia as PRIORITY (often overlooked). Watch-and-wait criteria clearly explained - appropriate for well child >2y with unilateral AOM. Delayed prescription strategy well-described (evidence-based approach). Consider adding brief mention of otitis externa differential (but TM exam distinguishes).

fracp_reviews.reviewer_credentials: FRACGP with pediatrics special interest, 14 years post-fellowship
fracp_reviews.clinical_accuracy: Accurate AOM management - appropriate use of watch-and-wait strategy and analgesia emphasis
fracp_reviews.difficulty_appropriate: Yes - Easy difficulty well-calibrated for GP/pediatrics
fracp_reviews.feedback: Good persona. Management pathway correct (analgesia first, watch-and-wait for well child >2y). Excellent inclusion of parent education on delayed prescription strategy. Red flags appropriately identified (mastoiditis, meningitis). Suggest mentioning 5-day antibiotic course explicitly (Australian guidelines updated from 10 days).

learning_objectives: Diagnose acute otitis media using 3 criteria (acute onset, middle ear effusion, inflammation)
Perform otoscopic examination (bulging TM, loss of light reflex, reduced mobility on pneumatic otoscopy)
Apply watch-and-wait strategy appropriately (well child >2y, unilateral AOM)
Prioritize analgesia over antibiotics (pain relief most important for symptom control)
Prescribe amoxicillin 50mg/kg/day TDS × 5 days (not 10 days) if antibiotics indicated
Educate parents on delayed prescription strategy (fill script only if no improvement 48h)
Recognize red flags requiring urgent referral (mastoiditis, meningitis)
Understand antibiotic stewardship (avoid unnecessary antibiotics to reduce resistance)
